Citi Experience 
 
This document is an attempt to make you aware of the mistakes people usually make 
and to help you not repeat them. Enjoy! 
 
Internship 
 
Selection Process: 
 
Round 1 (Test): 
 
A lot of branches were allowed to write the test (almost 400 participants). 
 
The test had the following sections -  
1) Logical Thinking 
2) English - (Reading and Grammar) 
3) Mathematics (basic till class-10) 
4) Programming (2 Questions -  only C/C++ & Java were allowed) 
 
The ​Programming section didn’t have much weightage​ (probably because, not 
many people solved both questions). 
Other sections were easy ​BUT​ they were easy for everyone. So, you need to be 
FAST​! 
 
I was Rank 3 on the test. The top-50 participants qualified to the next round 
 
Round 2 (Interview - Technical): 
 
The same day as the test, the ranks were declared and then the interviews were started 
(offline). 
 
Since I didn’t expect to get selected, I didn’t have a formal shirt or formal shoes. I also 
didn’t have a printed resume. If you are interviewing online, this won’t be a problem. 
But in general, ​during placement season, keep a shirt with one of your friends in 
the hostel​. I had to borrow and wore sports shoes.

Keep your resume clean and if possible a little colourful (when it comes to fonts). Use 
an only plain white background. It shouldn’t have more than two pages. 
 
The Interviews started and each participant was called in to sit alone in a cabin with 
the interviewer. The interviewer was very friendly. And there was essentially no 
pressure at the beginning. 
 
At this point, the interviewer looks at your resume. If you have a lot of projects they 
will concentrate on that throughout the interview. Otherwise, they will ask you which 
topics you are comfortable with (like OS, Data Structures & Algorithms, Theory of 
CS etc) and ask questions on those topics. 
 
He asked me a lot of questions about my projects (Thanks to ​SRA​). About 
implementation and which technologies I used. Also, ​why I used the technologies​. 
Make sure you know the answer to that. 
 
After this conceptual part of the interview is done, the interviewer will ask which 
language or databases you are most comfortable with. I answered Python and Mongo. 
He asked why I prefer each. Then, he gave a DSA question that was ​“Find the 
smallest common substring given two strings”. ​It is actually a very common 
question, but I didn’t remember how to solve using DP since I hadn’t revised. So, I 
asked him if he wanted the Iterative or the Recursive answer. And to my bad luck, he 
said “Iterative”. And I had to solve it that way, which I did after squirming for long. 
Then also solved in DP. After every loop/function that you write on paper, tell the 
interviewer why you wrote it. 
 
They also ask random questions like “What do you think about the dark web?”, “Have 
you ever tried working with RegEx?” 
 
Moral of the story: Be confident (not overconfident). Only name topics that you know, 
and are confident in. Prepare well for the interview, don’t be like me. Whenever you 
are asked an algorithm’s question ​Think Out Loud. ​Let the interviewer know about 
your thought process. 
 
Round 3 (Interview - HR): 
 
The HR interview for me was more difficult than the technical one. They asked why I 
had a low GPA but had time for projects. They also asked:

1) How would the people around you describe you? 
2) What according to you is Leadership? (It’s okay to get political here, it lets 
them know that you are aware of what’s going on around you) 
3) In New York City, how will you distribute Barbers?  
New York City has a grid layout (with streets and avenues). What factors will 
you take into consideration to distributes Barbers evenly throughout the city? 
Answer: ​Population Density, Affordability (expensive on the Upper East and 
cheap in Brooklyn), Gender of the population etc. 
4) Why Citi?  
5) I had worked with startups so they asked - will you be able to adjust in an 
MNC after working in such free environments? 
 
So, that’s it. The same day by night, 10 people got internships. 5 Girls and 5 Boys 
(From IT, CS, Production, Electrical - I think). 
 
 
Internship Experience: 
 
Environment: 
I haven’t come across a single intern that had a toxic work environment at Citi, unlike 
in some other companies. 
The HR department is great, and so are the leaders. Everyone was treated well. 
 
Stipend: 
Our seniors were paid 40k/month.  They worked for 2 months. I think you’re 
supposed to arrange apartments/hostels on your own.  Our seniors had a week’s stay at 
a hotel, I think. 
Due to COVID, we only worked for one month but got paid for 2. And we worked 
from home. 
 
Project: 
They either made teams of 6/7 or 3. And they usually ensure that people from the 
same college were together so that we're already gelled.  
Since we were working from home we used GitHub and HackerEarth for 
collaboration.

We worked on a Java Application and the main concentration was on the Algorithm 
Development and not the Application Development. There were 2 teams of 3 working 
on the same problem, in parallel. 
We had 3 mentors and they were very supportive and very helpful. 
 
PPO: 
My BU was TTS, it's the most populated so the competition for PPO is usually higher. 
There is a ppt at the end of every week, and you need to perform well if you want a 
PPO. The last one is the most important one, in which you will have external judges. 
You have to work hard every week and show your progress. 
Keep your PPT clean and readable. Don’t complicate it too much, cuz you have only a 
fixed amount of time to present it. 
Out of 10 people, 9 got PPOs. If you don’t want a PPO, inform your HR in advance, 
cuz if you get it you can’t reject it.
